title.en: Makonaima's Son and the Wondrous Tree (Akawai)
title.zh: 馬科納伊瑪之子與神樹（阿卡瓦版）

region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'The First Man and Animals: Primitive State'

summary.en: First the Acawoi narrator told how beasts and birds were made: how the Mighty, their Creator, gave them laws to be obeyed, made them of one speech, bade them live in unity. That there might be no oppression, man was made and placed o'er all: that first man, of wise discretion, 'Makonaima's son' we call — just as well as kind was he; all obeyed him lovingly. Ere the sun's bright rays were burning all dispersed in forests near; with the cool of day returning, glad his loving call to hear: each one of his food would bring — homage paid to man, their king. Then 'tis said, great Makonaima made for them a wondrous tree, capped with clouds like high Roraima, bearing fruits abundantly — every kind — the meed to be of their love and loyalty: 'Ahkoo,' the agouti, the noble tree found, and our first man alone brought it down to the ground, the animals helping him in planting around.
summary.zh: 阿卡瓦敘事者言：造物主造獸鳥，定律令之，使同語而相睦。又造人以統御，免相凌；首人者，『馬科納伊瑪之子』也，智而仁，眾皆悅服。日出而散於林，暮歸而樂其召；各獻其食——王乎人矣。大神馬科納伊瑪復為之造神樹，雲冠其頂，如羅賴馬之高，百果具備，以償其忠愛。刺鼠阿庫先得之；首人獨力伐之，眾獸助其播種。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose and read critically — the 'unity' framing bears missionary coloring.

passages.text: First, my Acawoi narrator told how beasts and birds were made: how the Mighty, their Creator, gave them laws to be obeyed; made them of one speech to be, bade them live in unity. That there might be no oppression, man was made, and placed o'er all. That first man, of wise discretion, 'Makonaima's son' we call: just, as well as kind, was he; all obeyed him lovingly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First Man and Animals'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ere the sun's bright rays were burning, all dispersed in forests near; with the cool of day returning, glad his loving call to hear: each one of his food would bring — homage paid to man, their king. No great trouble or disaster could oppress them or annoy; for the man, their gentle master, in their good placed all his joy. Then, 'tis said, great Makonaima made for them a wondrous tree, capped with clouds, like high Roraima, bearing fruits abundantly — every kind — the meed to be of their love and loyalty: 'Ahkoo,' the agouti, the noble tree found, and our first man alone brought it down to the ground, the animals helping him in planting around.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The First Man and Animals'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkey and the Basket: the Akawai Flood

region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'The Monkey's Exploit'

summary.en: The beasts and the birds were industrious all, till Iwarreka — so the brown monkey we call — to the spirit of play and sheer mischief gave way: 'He pulls at our tails, or nips with his nails.' So the master passed sentence: 'Iwarreka, leave us, and work by thyself; go to yon spring, and thence, in a basket, fresh water to bring.' When the tree was cut down the good master soon found swelling waters within, and there abound those fishes which now swim in rivers around: 'I will spread them; every river shall share.' He found that those waters, ere next rise of sun, o'er the world all around were preparing to run; so with dexterous hands a wide basket he made which, inverted, he over the hollow stump laid — such was its virtue that, while it remained as he placed it, the fountain within was restrained. Iwarreka, meanwhile, obedience shirking, was lurking near: 'The choicest of fruits our sly master hides there.' With a light spring he stands on the margin and raises the basket with pilfering hands — one moment, no more, for a terrible flood, bursting forth, sends him rolling in water and mud. 'See the water pouring over the side! See, the fishes are all swimming down with the tide. See, the stump and the roots are all forced from the ground, and the land disappears as the waters flow round!' So the man leads the way to a tall hill with high rocks and cocorite trees: the birds fly up first, then the opossum, coati, and monkeys all, tails curled round their necks; such a rain succeeded as none before knew, and the man let fall the seeds of the cocorite tree, to tell by the splash where the water might be — at length it seemed gone; then they ate of the palm-fruits and welcomed the dawn.
summary.zh: 百獸皆勤，惟棕猴伊瓦雷卡頑皮擾眾：『拽吾尾，齧吾膚。』主乃判曰：『爾獨往彼泉，以籃取水。』樹伐而泉湧於樁中，魚盈焉；主曰：『當分之於諸河。』知水將氾濫，乃織巨籃倒覆樁上，泉遂塞。猴覘之，竊發其籃——洪暴出，猴滾於水泥。眾驚呼：『水漫矣！魚隨流去！樹樁拔，陸地沒！』主引眾至高山，有柯基里棕與巖穴；鳥先登，負鼠浣熊繼之，群猴繞其身。暴雨三日不見日；主投棕實測水深——水終退，眾食棕果而迎旦。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Flood-cluster record.

passages.text: The beasts and the birds were industrious all, till 'Iwarreka' — so the brown monkey we call — to the spirit of play and sheer mischief gave way; then he plagued and tormented the rest all the day. 'He pulls at our tails, or nips with his nails, and will bite us severely when any trick fails.' So the master passed sentence on that wicked elf: 'Iwarreka, leave us, and work by thyself; it will keep thee from mischief to go to yon spring, and thence, in a basket, fresh water to bring.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Monkey's Exploit'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the tree was cut down the good master soon found swelling waters within: and he saw there abound those fishes which now swim in rivers around. 'Though more labour for me, this a blessing will be: I will spread them — every river shall share.' And he found that those waters, ere next rise of sun, o'er the world all around were preparing to run. Then with dexterous hands a wide basket he made which, inverted, he over the hollow stump laid; and such was its virtue that, while it remained as he placed it, the fountain within was restrained.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Monkey's Exploit'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Iwarreka, meanwhile, obedience shirking, had given up working, and near to the spot at that time he was lurking: 'The choicest of fruits our sly master hides there. I will take while I may, now they all are away.' So, with a light spring, on the margin he stands; the basket he raises with pilfering hands — one moment, no more — for a terrible flood bursting forth sends him rolling in water and mud. 'See the water pouring over the side! See, the stump and the roots are all forced from the ground, and the land disappears as the waters flow round!' So the man leads the way till before him he sees a tall hill, with high rocks, and some cocorite trees: the birds fly up first; and then up the tree go the opossum, coati, and monkeys all. Such a rain then succeeded as none before knew: the man let fall the seeds of the cocorite tree, to tell by the splash where the water might be; he at length found it lower, at last it seemed gone — then they ate of the palm-fruits, and welcomed the dawn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Monkey's Exploit'; not verbatim.

title.en: Mishaps of the Flood: the Howler, the Trumpeter, and the Tongueless Alligator
title.zh: 洪水之厄：吼猴、鶴鳥與無舌之鱷

region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'Mishaps'

summary.en: Thus the man, beasts, and birds were preserved, though cold, wet, and hungry — but some met with troubles of which their children bear tokens to this very day. First the 'baboon', the great howling monkey: his voice, we are told, ere he climbed up that tree was more pleasant to hear than his person to see; he began first to roar as he felt his heart fail, when those waters were wetting his feet and his tail — though his throat did not burst with the strain of those cries, it then grew to be twice its original size. The trumpeter bird, with the others, heard the man bid all keep their places till he should have found if danger awaited on the damp ground — yet he would not from getting down first be deterred: 'Yahgahmi, beware!' said the man with a frown, as into a nest of fierce ants he flew down; each leg was a stick, though once fairly thick, for those ants had deprived it of all they could pick. Then, the fire kindled by friction, the marudi pecked up the red coal from the ground, mistaking it for an insect, and away the bird flew — his throat, much inflamed, took a fiery glow from the coal he pecked up below. And before the man stood the first alligator, come forth from the mud — well-conducted then, come to pay his respects; but the rest, who disliked him, said 'He took the fire!' and the man, cold and weary, gave way to his ire: forcing open his mouth to search there, found his tongue in the way — and pulled out the tongue! The reptile, disgusted, went tongueless away, and from that time made war on all creatures; alligators — wanting tongues — show and share their father's wrongs.
summary.zh: 人獸鳥雖得全，然各有厄，其子孫至今猶帶其痕。吼猴——『狒狒』也——洪水浸其足尾，懼而大吼；其吼聲使其喉腫至二倍——今之巨喉是也。鶴鳥不聽主命，先下而入蟻塚；主呼『雅加米慎之』——其脛被蟻齧細如枝。摩擦既得火，馬魯迪鳥誤紅炭為蟲而啄之，喉赤如火——至今猶然。首鱷自泥出，本恭謹來賀；眾獸誣其竊火；主怒，開其口而拔其舌——鱷自此無舌，與百獸永戰。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Fire-theft cluster record.

passages.text: Thus the man, beasts, and birds were preserved, as we see, though cold, wet, and hungry, of course they would be. But some met with troubles, of which, sages say, their children bear tokens to this very day. And first, the 'baboon', as your Creoles now call the great howling monkey, the reddest of all: his voice, we are told, ere he climbed up that tree was more pleasant to hear than his person to see. He began first to roar, as he felt his heart fail, when those waters were wetting his feet and his tail, and he knew they would drown him if they should prevail. Though his throat did not burst with the strain of those cries, it then grew to be twice its original size!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Mishaps'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He bade all keep their places till he should have found if danger awaited them on the damp ground; and the trumpeter bird with the others then heard, yet he would not from getting down first be deterred. 'Yahgahmi, beware!' said the man, with a frown, as into a nest of fierce ants he flew down. Alas, for the bird! Each leg was a stick (though once fairly thick), for those ants had deprived it of all they could pick. Having cleared off the ants, the long-suffering man kindled a fire by friction — and, while he looked round for fuel, the marudi pecked up the red coal from the ground, mistaking it for an insect, and away the bird flew: his throat, much inflamed, took a fiery glow from the coal he pecked up below.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Mishaps'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The man looked for his fire; and before him then stood the first alligator, come forth from the mud. That reptile was then well-conducted, they say, and had come his respects to the master to pay. But the rest, who disliked him, said 'He took the fire!' and the man, cold and weary, gave way to his ire: forcing open his mouth, to search there (he was wrong), found his tongue in the way — and he pulled out the tongue! O sad were the mishaps of that fatal day: the reptile, disgusted, went (tongueless) away, and from that time made war on all creatures, they say. Alligators — wanting tongues — show (and share) their father's wrongs.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Mishaps'; not verbatim.

title.en: End of the Primitive State: the Guardian Ascends the Cliff
title.zh: 太古之終：守護者登崖而去

region.zh: 羅賴馬附近峭壁（象徵定位）

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'End of Primitive State'

summary.en: Then the birds and beasts, rebelling, soon forsook their guardian mild; pride of freedom in them swelling, in the forests all went wild — there their children bear tokens of their ancestry. Free as air then roved those creatures till they saw, with savage natures, beasts of prey and hunters come; felt their bloody, cruel reign, wished their guardian back again. Wondrous deeds of that good man could be told — but every day bad men sought the good to slay. Envy made their hatred stronger: he was forced to leave them there. Yet, when they were suffering hunger, sent for them his bread to share — they, partaking of his food, sought again to shed his blood! Then, a precipice ascending, on that cliff immense and high, with a faithful few attending, he was seen beneath the sky. Evil men he left below to suffer want and woe; he left no track behind him, all who sought to climb would fall — 'twas like high Roraima's wall: nay, since none now know its name, some may think that cliff the same.
summary.zh: 鳥獸終叛其溫良之主，縱傲而狂於林——其子孫至今猶帶先祖之徵。既而見猛獸獵人之至，始悔而思其主。惡人日謀殺善人；妒火愈烈，主遂去之。然眾饑時，仍召之共享其餅；食畢又欲害其命！主乃率忠從數人登絕壁，高聳天際。惡人留於下界受苦；主去無跡，攀者皆墜——壁如羅賴馬之牆；以其名今不可知，或以為即彼山也。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose.

passages.text: Then the birds and beasts, rebelling, soon forsook their guardian mild; pride of freedom in them swelling, in the forests all went wild: there their children bear, we see, tokens of their ancestry. Free as air then roved those creatures, till they saw, with savage natures, beasts of prey and hunters come; felt their bloody, cruel reign, wished their guardian back again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'End of Primitive State'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Every day bad men sought the good to slay. Envy made their hatred stronger: he was forced to leave them there. Yet, when they were suffering hunger, sent for them his bread to share — they, partaking of his food, sought again to shed his blood! Then, a precipice ascending, on that cliff immense and high (with a faithful few attending), he was seen beneath the sky. Evil men he left below, there to suffer want and woe; and he left no track behind him — all who sought to climb would fall; none could follow there to find him: 'twas like high Roraima's wall!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'End of Primitive State'; not verbatim.

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'Their War with the Caribs: The Surprise on the Cuyuni'

summary.en: My ancestors once dwelt, our legends say, where Mazaruni cuts his rugged way from mountains where stupendous rocks abound; north of that river my forefathers dwelt in days of old, and no great evils felt — 'twas by the Caribs they were forced to flee. Great was the horror when a cry at night proclaimed the Caribs nigh: they ravaged the neighbouring land, and killed their captives in their rage — maimed some boys and impaled some, to show their vengeance had not failed. Our warriors met, an angry train, that ere the Caribs came again they might for them prepare; the old chief said: 'We'll save the Caribs half their walk by meeting them midway!' Our warriors to Cuyuni go, and from its banks behold the foe coming before the breeze. Close amidst the trees they hide themselves and see them land; their foes, reclining on the strand, then eat and take their ease — no scout, no watch! Hark, that fierce cry: as up they start, at each man flies a fatal dart — one half their death-wounds bear. No valour can regain the day; their men will for no mercy pray, and ours no mercy show: soon, half in water, half on land, two hundred corpses line the strand.
summary.zh: 吾祖舊居馬扎魯尼之岸；加勒比迫之而徙。一夜號哭報敵至；彼等肆虐鄉鄰，怒戮俘虜——殘害男孩以逞其恨。吾眾集而備之；老酋曰：『吾儕當迎擊於中途，免其半途之勞！』眾至庫尤尼，匿於樹間，見敵登岸，臥沙而食，無偵無哨。一聲呼嘯，毒箭齊發；半數立斃。餘者奔舟，莫能返戰。俄而屍橫兩百，半在水中半在沙。

sensitivity.note: Akawai historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; read critically.

passages.text: My ancestors once dwelt, our legends say, where Masaruni cuts his rugged way from mountains, where stupendous rocks abound, by falls prodigious, to this lower ground. North of that river my forefathers dwelt in days of old, and no great evils felt — 'twas by the Caribs they were forced to flee. Great was the horror, when a cry at night proclaimed the Caribs nigh! They came, a numerous train; and ravaged through the neighbouring land, where our bold brethren made a stand — some Caribs there were slain. Nought could their comrades' wrath assuage, who killed their captives in their rage; then, seeing boys remain, they maimed some, and some impaled, to show their vengeance had not failed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Surprise on the Cuyuni'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Our warriors met, an angry train, that ere the Caribs came again they might for them prepare. 'We'll save the Caribs half their walk by meeting them midway!' Our warriors to Cuyuni go, and from its banks behold the foe coming before the breeze: their frail, but numerous barques draw nigh. Close amidst the trees they hide themselves and see them land; their foes, reclining on the strand, then eat and take their ease — no scout, no watch! They know no fear, nor think a deadly ambush near. Hark, that fierce cry! As up they start, at each man flies a fatal dart: one half their death-wounds bear. No valour can regain the day; their men will for no mercy pray, and ours no mercy show: soon, half in water, half on land, two hundred corpses line the strand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Surprise on the Cuyuni'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Siege of the Fortified House: 'They Burned the House — and Fled!'

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'Siege of the Fortified House'

summary.en: Again the Caribs, strong and bold, returned, as our old chief foretold: 'For each warrior we have slain, be sure, when they shall come again, the Caribs will bring ten.' When the foe drew near, to help him he saw few appear. 'This place is lost,' the chieftain said, 'but they shall surely pay full dearly, with their warriors dead, for what they get this day.' To the women: 'Wait till the fight is high, and foes engaged, then when I give the signal quickly fly through the tunnel's friendly shade.' The Caribs to the assault drew nigh: from bulwarks strong swift arrows flew, tipped with wourali all; their best men came with furious rush; some dug beneath the wooden wall and made a hole through which to crawl — but those who entered that way all entered but to die! Then flaming arrows swiftly poured upon the loop-holed sides and thatched roof; soon roof and sides were in a blaze, and they raised their joyful shouts of 'Victory!' — but quiet, save the fiery roar, they found all things remain: our men had gone down through the floor, and soon would reach Puruni's shore, not to return again. The flaming house burned to the ground; but no charred skeletons were found: all said, 'Tis sorcery indeed, such as none knew before!' — so to this day our people say: 'They burned the house — and fled!'
summary.zh: 加勒比復至，如其老酋所料：『殺其一，必來其十！』援兵不至；酋曰：『此地將失，然彼必以戰士之死償今日之得！』婦人待戰酣，聞號而遁地道之蔭。加勒比攻寨；寨中箭皆塗阿拉里毒，中者立斃；掘牆入者入即死！縱火焚其茅頂板壁——敵歡呼得勝——而寨中寂然惟火聲；吾人已穿地而出，將達普魯尼之岸矣。屋焚為灰而無骸；眾曰：『此真妖術也！』故至今吾人猶言：『彼等焚屋而遁！』

sensitivity.note: Akawai historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; read critically.

passages.text: Again the Caribs, strong and bold, returned, as our old chief foretold, who, speaking to his men, said: 'For each warrior we have slain, be sure, when they shall come again, the Caribs will bring ten.' It was so: when the foe drew near, to help him he saw few appear. 'This place is lost,' the chieftain said, 'but they shall surely pay full dearly, with their warriors dead, for what they get this day!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Siege of the Fortified House'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then to the women: 'Ye shall live; wait till the fight is high, and foes engaged, then, when I give the signal, quickly fly through the tunnel's friendly shade; fly silent through each forest glade — utter no timid cry!' The Caribs to the assault drew nigh and scanned the place with curious eye, but saw their leaders fall. From bulwarks strong swift arrows flew — tipped with wourali all! To storm the place forth from the bush came their best men with furious rush; some dug beneath the wooden wall and made a hole through which to crawl: but those who entered that way, all there entered but to die!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Siege of the Fortified House'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then flaming arrows swiftly poured upon the loop-holed sides of board, and that thatched roof on high: soon roof and sides were in a blaze, and they their joyful shouts could raise of 'Victory!' the cry. They burst the enclosure, waiting there the shrieks of agony and fear — but quiet, save the fiery roar, they found all things remain: our men had gone down through the floor, and soon would reach Puruni's shore, not to return again. The flaming house burned to the ground; but no charred skeletons were found. All said: 'Tis sorcery indeed, such as none knew before!' So when our warriors came, they found but blackened ruins on the ground, and many new-made graves around, filled with the Carib dead — and so to this day our people say: 'They burned the house — and fled!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Siege of the Fortified House'; not verbatim.

title.en: Ekahruwa's Duel: the Old Man and the Sting-Ray Arrow
title.zh: 埃卡魯瓦之決鬥：老翁與魟刺之箭

region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼-普魯尼河

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'Civil Strife: The Duel'

summary.en: On the Puruni, loved of all, dwelt one whom we will 'Koë' call; a chief was staying at his home, a friend from Mazaruni come — there the loved guest fell sick and died. Ekahruwa, the dead man's son, by sorcery led, had vowed to cleave the hoary head as a most righteous deed: 'By dreams and secret arts I know that Koë my father slew.' He came with desperadoes, found Koë gone — 'Then you for him must die!' — cruelly slew the neighbours, took the girls and spoil. The Puruni men pursued, set the maidens free; and Ekahruwa, calling his foes one at a time, slew nine — 'Still is my vengeance unfulfilled: I come, and that old man shall die!' Soon he came again with a numerous train from red Roraima's wall; the chiefs mediated in vain. Then forth there came the old man with the good white head: 'No man for me shall fight, and fall by this proud boaster's hand; this hand, though weak, may do me right: a fair field now command!' He laid down the club he once could wield, took but one arrow, and tranquilly remained; his arrows he put aside from others swerving wide; when the strong man saw the sting-ray's deadly spine on the opposing reed, he for the first time doubted which of the two must die — then, with a flying bound, one piercing shriek: the strong man lies upon the ground, reached with his last death spring. 'My brother did to death consign some of your men, in number ten; while of his men you killed but nine — the deaths are equal. Peace be between us from this day!'
summary.zh: 普魯尼河畔有老者科埃；其友自馬扎魯尼來，客死其家。死者之子埃卡魯瓦恃巫術，誓斬白髮翁——『以夢與秘術知父為科埃所害。』率暴徒屠鄰人，擄其女。普魯尼人追而釋女；埃卡魯瓦獨戰九人皆斃——『吾仇未報：老翁必死！』再率大軍自紅羅賴馬而來。白髮翁自出曰：『毋人為我戰而隕；此手雖弱，足伸吾冤。』棄其戰棒，惟執一箭，靜立於野。敵箭四射，翁皆閃避；強者見其箭鏃為魟刺——大駭——終躍而撲；一聲哀號，強者倒地。其弟曰：『吾兄殺汝十人，汝殺其九，今又斃之——其數等矣。自今日起，兩族罷兵！』

sensitivity.note: Akawai historical legend recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; read critically.

passages.text: On the Puruni, loved of all, dwelt one whom we will 'Koë' call: a chief was staying at his home, a friend from Masaruni come, in rank and years the same. There the loved guest fell sick and died. Ekahruwa, so he was called, from no fierce crime would shrink appalled, but breathed forth death and flame. Ekahruwa, by sorcery led, had vowed to cleave the hoary head as a most righteous deed: 'No evidence I show; by dreams and secret arts I know that Koë my father slew.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Duel'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Of Masaruni men a band, the desperadoes of the land, hastened to march beneath his command. They to Koë's place had come: there, finding he had left his home, 'Has he escaped indeed — the hoary wretch I doomed to bleed? Then you for him must die!' So cruelly those men he slew, and would have killed the women too: 'Ten men this day we've helped you slay; it is enough.' Take now the girls and spoil away. The Puruni men pursued and set the maidens free: 'Nine men I've seen around me fall, by your sharp arrows slain. Still is my vengeance unfulfilled, and I must come again. I come — and that old man shall die; if him you screen, none living shall remain!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Duel'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He came again with a numerous train from red Roraima. Then forth came the old man with the good white head: No man for me shall fight, and fall by this proud boaster hand! This hand, though weak, may do me right; a fair field now command. He lays down the club he once could wield, but neer shall wield again; sees him but one arrow take, and tranquilly remain. The foe made feints and circled round; the old man covered him with steady eye, till the strong man saw the sting-ray deadly spine on the opposing reed, and for the first time doubted which of the two must die. Straight he came with flying bound; the arrow left the string; one piercing shriek: the strong man lies upon the ground. The deaths are equal, and peace is made between the clans from this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Duel'; not verbatim.

title.en: Kanaima: the Vow, the Jaguar, and the Blood at the Grave
title.zh: 卡奈瑪：毒誓、美洲豹與墓前之血

region.en: From Roraima to the Eastern sea (Akawai)
region.zh: 自羅賴馬至東海（阿卡瓦）

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part IV 'Legends of the Acawoios', 'Kanaima'

summary.en: From the base of high Roraima to the widespread Eastern sea, votaries of dread Kanaima track their victims secretly. Deadly vow must each fulfil, real or fancied foe to kill: he who that dread vow is taking, family and friends must leave — wife and children all forsaking, no discharge can he receive; still around his victim's way, hovering night and day to slay. Stealthily each step he traces, hiding till he strikes the blow; poison in the mouth he places of his victim, lying low; then, if found with swollen tongue, none will know who did him wrong. When the grave has closed upon him the destroyer hovers round: dread Kanaima's spell is on him, by it he must still be bound, till he pierce with pointed wood through the grave, and taste the blood — stern Kanaima thus appeasing, who withdraws his direful aid. One who passed on the Upper Demerara in 1865 was fresh from slaughter, hastening home again: a feathered crown adorned his head — bright red spots his skin o'erspread — spots, to show that, nightly ranging (so their sorcerers declare), he, into a jaguar changing, could his victims seize and tear, as the were-wolf of the East prowls on human flesh to feast. Should the victim escape him living, the spell upon him lies; mad, he wanders till he dies.
summary.zh: 自羅賴馬之麓至東海之濱，卡奈瑪之毒誓者密跡獵其仇。立誓者必離家室，誓成方免；日夜伺於仇人之途，忍而待機。毒置於垂死者口中；舌腫而莫知誰弒。墓既閉，報仇者猶繞之：卡奈瑪之咒縛其身，必以尖木刺墓、飲血乃解。1865年上德梅拉拉河有帶血而歸者：羽冠在首，肌有紅斑——薩滿言其夜能化美洲豹，噬其仇人，如東方之狼人也。仇若得脫，咒不離身；狂走至死。

sensitivity.note: Akawai kanaima tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; the blood-feud practice is described from a missionary perspective — read critically; no restricted ritual detail included.

passages.text: From the base of high Roraima to the widespread Eastern sea, votaries of dread Kanaima track their victims secretly. Deadly vow must each fulfil, real or fancied foe to kill. He who that dread vow is taking, family and friends must leave; wife and children all forsaking, no discharge can he receive: still around his victim's way, hovering night and day to slay. If the victim, warned of danger, to some other place should fly, soon the assassin, though a stranger, will to that retreat draw nigh — patiently he bides his time, waiting to commit the crime.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Kanaima'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Stealthily each step he traces, hiding till he strikes the blow; poison in the mouth he places of his victim, lying low: then, if found with swollen tongue, none will know who did him wrong. When the grave has closed upon him, the destroyer hovers round: dread Kanaima's spell is on him, by it he must still be bound, till he pierce, with pointed wood, through the grave, and taste the blood — stern Kanaima thus appeasing, who withdraws his direful aid; all his horrid influence ceasing when that offering has been made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Kanaima'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One, who passed us on the water, had his victim lately slain; there, triumphant, fresh from slaughter, he was hastening home again: a feathered crown adorned his head — bright red spots his skin o'erspread — spots, to show that, nightly ranging (so their sorcerers declare), he, into a jaguar changing, could his victims seize and tear, as the were-wolf of the East prowls, on human flesh to feast. Should the victim escape him living, he, no horrid offering giving, finds Kanaima on him stay: still the spell upon him lies; mad, he wanders till he dies.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Kanaima'; not verbatim.
